MUQATIL:3:116-117/r1.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:3:116-117/r1.speaker: author
MUQATIL:3:116-117/r1.claim: Lower-ranking Jews spent food and fruit for their leaders Ka'b b. al-Ashraf and his companions, hoping for the afterlife despite their disbelief.

MUQATIL:3:116-117/r2.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:3:116-117/r2.speaker: author
MUQATIL:3:116-117/r2.claim: Their spending, including that of Meccan unbelievers, was destroyed like a freezing wind that ruins the crop of people who wronged themselves.

MUQATIL:3:116-117/r3.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:3:116-117/r3.speaker: author
MUQATIL:3:116-117/r3.claim: God did not wrong them by refusing their expenditure; they wronged themselves through disbelief.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p109/r1.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p109/r1.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p109/r1.claim: Ṣirr is cold; the text also mentions a prohibition concerning locusts killed by cold.

TAB-FULL:v5p703/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v5p703/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v5p703/r1.claim: The spent wealth of disbelievers, even when given as devotion, is annulled because they deny God's oneness and the Messenger; it is like a freezing wind destroying a sinful people's hoped-for harvest.

TAB-FULL:v5p703/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v5p703/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v5p703/r2.claim: The comparison concerns God's cancellation of their reward, as the context makes clear, like the parable of the person who kindled a fire.

TAB-FULL:v5p703/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v5p703/r3.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v5p703/r3.claim: Mujāhid takes the spending to mean a disbeliever's expenditure in this world.

TAB-FULL:v5p703/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v5p703/r4.speaker: السدي
TAB-FULL:v5p703/r4.claim: Al-Suddī instead interprets it as words spoken without inward belief, rendered fruitless by associating partners with God.

TAB-FULL:v5p703/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v5p703/r5.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v5p703/r5.claim: Ṣirr means intense cold, caused by a fierce north wind.

TAB-FULL:v5p707/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v5p707/r1.speaker: عكرمة
TAB-FULL:v5p707/r1.claim: ʿIkrima glosses ṣirr as severe cold; Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatāda, al-Rabīʿ, al-Suddī, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk likewise identify it as cold or severe cold.

TAB-FULL:v5p707/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v5p707/r2.speaker: ابن زيد
TAB-FULL:v5p707/r2.claim: Ibn Zayd says the cold wind destroys crops and is called ḍarīb when it leaves plants burned by freezing cold.

TAB-FULL:v5p707/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v5p707/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v5p707/r3.claim: God does not cancel their reward unjustly: their deeds lacked monotheistic sincerity and belief in the messengers despite prior warning; their unbelief makes them responsible for punishment.

ZAJJAJ:v1p460/r5.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v1p460/r5.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v1p460/r5.claim: The harm of their spending against the Prophet resembles a killing cold that destroys the crop of people who wronged themselves.

ZAJJAJ:v1p460/r6.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v1p460/r6.speaker: قال بعضهم
ZAJJAJ:v1p460/r6.claim: Some say the example refers to Meccans who pooled money to oppose the Prophet; others take the spending as their deeds in idolatry.

ZAJJAJ:v1p460/r7.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v1p460/r7.speaker: قال بعضهم
ZAJJAJ:v1p460/r7.claim: Another linguistic possibility takes ṣirr as a sound, the noise of fire consuming the crop, which the author says is not impossible.

ZAJJAJ:v1p460/r8.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v1p460/r8.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v1p460/r8.claim: Spending to support hostility against religion harms and destroys its proponents in this life and the next.

IBNABIHATIM:v3p741#2/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v3p741#2/r1.speaker: مجاهد
IBNABIHATIM:v3p741#2/r1.claim: Mujahid says the spending in this worldly life means the spending of a disbeliever; Hasan and al-Suddi are also reported to agree.

IBNABIHATIM:v3p741#2/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v3p741#2/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v3p741#2/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses the wind's صر as cold; similar readings are reported from several early authorities.

IBNABIHATIM:v3p741#2/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v3p741#2/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v3p741#2/r3.claim: In another view, Ibn Abbas says صر means fire; one report from Mujahid agrees.

IBNABIHATIM:v3p741#2/r4.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v3p741#2/r4.speaker: عطاء
IBNABIHATIM:v3p741#2/r4.claim: Ata says the wind contains cold and ice.

IBNABIHATIM:v3p741#2/r5.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v3p741#2/r5.speaker: السدي
IBNABIHATIM:v3p741#2/r5.claim: Al-Suddi says the disbelievers' unaccepted spending resembles a crop ruined by freezing wind: their associationism destroys their deeds.

IBNABIHATIM:v3p741#2/r6.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v3p741#2/r6.speaker: الحسن
IBNABIHATIM:v3p741#2/r6.claim: Hasan says the wind ruined the field by stripping and burning it.

IBNABIHATIM:v3p741#2/r7.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v3p741#2/r7.speaker: عبد الرحمن بن زيد بن أسلم
IBNABIHATIM:v3p741#2/r7.claim: Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd says God disavows responsibility for punishing earlier nations because they wronged themselves.

IBNABIHATIM:v3p742/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v3p742/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v3p742/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses people wronging themselves as harming themselves.

THALABI:v3p133/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v3p133/r1.speaker: يمان
THALABI:v3p133/r1.claim: Yamān interprets the spending as Abū Sufyān and his companions' expenditures at Badr and Uḥud in opposition to the Messenger.

THALABI:v3p133/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v3p133/r2.speaker: مقاتل
THALABI:v3p133/r2.claim: Muqātil says it means the lower-ranking Jews' spending on their leaders and scholars, including Kaʿb and his companions.

THALABI:v3p133/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v3p133/r3.speaker: مجاهد
THALABI:v3p133/r3.claim: Mujāhid takes the verse to mean all unbelievers' worldly spending and charity.

THALABI:v3p133/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v3p133/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
THALABI:v3p133/r4.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says ṣirr is the killing hot simoom, from which God created the jinn; Ibn Kaysān says it is a wind with sound and fire, while most commentators say it is intense cold.

THALABI:v3p133/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v3p133/r5.speaker: author
THALABI:v3p133/r5.claim: The people who wronged themselves are the crop's owners, because they disbelieved, sinned, and withheld what was due to God.

THALABI:v3p133/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v3p133/r6.speaker: author
THALABI:v3p133/r6.claim: Unbelievers' spending is like a cold wind or fire destroying a crop: its hoped-for benefit disappears when needed, and God has not wronged them; they wrong themselves by disbelief, sin, and withholding God's due.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p523/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p523/r1.speaker: يمان
WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p523/r1.claim: Yaman says the verse concerns Abu Sufyan and the polytheists funding opposition to the Prophet at Badr and Uhud.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p523/r10.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p523/r10.speaker: ابن كيسان
WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p523/r10.claim: Ibn Kaysan and Ibn al-Anbari take ṣirr to mean fire.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p523/r11.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p523/r11.speaker: مجاهد
WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p523/r11.claim: Mujahid has the fire interpretation in Ibn Abi Najih's report.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p523/r12.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p523/r12.speaker: ابن الأنباري
WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p523/r12.claim: Ibn al-Anbari links the name of fire as ṣirr to its sound as it blazes.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p523/r13.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p523/r13.speaker: الزجاج
WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p523/r13.claim: Al-Zajjaj allows the fire interpretation and says a flame's sound is called ṣarr, with 'door creak' and a bird's cry as lexical parallels.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p523/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p523/r2.speaker: مقاتل
WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p523/r2.claim: Muqatil identifies the spending as that of lower-ranking Jews on their religious scholars.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p523/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p523/r3.speaker: مجاهد
WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p523/r3.claim: Mujahid takes it broadly as all spending and charitable giving by disbelievers in worldly life.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p523/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p523/r4.speaker: الزجاج
WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p523/r4.claim: Al-Zajjaj says it covers every expenditure meant to display hostility toward religion.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p523/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p523/r5.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p523/r5.claim: Mathal denotes a likeness made familiar like an established sign through repeated use; an omitted phrase, the destruction of their spending, parallels the wind's destruction of crops.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p523/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p523/r6.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p523/r6.claim: Most exegetes and linguists, including Ibn Abbas in Ataa's report, Qatada, al-Rabi, al-Suddi, and Ibn Zayd, define ṣirr as intense cold.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p523/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p523/r7.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p523/r7.claim: Spending against religion ruins the disbelievers' deeds in the afterlife just as the cold wind ruins the crop it strikes.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p523/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p523/r8.speaker: الزجاج
WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p523/r8.claim: Al-Zajjaj explains that their spending harms them just as the wind harms the crop.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p523/r9.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p523/r9.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p523/r9.claim: Ibn Abbas also explains ṣirr as the lethal, hot simoom winds.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p528/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p528/r1.speaker: الراعي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p528/r1.claim: Al-Rai's line describes a harsh summer wind, supporting the hot-wind interpretation and its audible quality.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p528/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p528/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p528/r2.claim: On this reading, the wind is a scorching wind like fire that burns the crop, or a noisy fire; the sound sense also suits hot simoom winds.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p528/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p528/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p528/r3.claim: A report through al-Suddi and Abu Malik from Ibn Abbas says the wind contains fire.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p528/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p528/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p528/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas says the people wronged themselves by denying God's favor; others explain their wrong as unbelief and disobedience.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p528/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p528/r5.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p528/r5.claim: God does not wrong them: whatever He does with His creation is just, since He acts within His own dominion.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p528/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p528/r6.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v5p528/r6.claim: People wrong themselves through unbelief and disobedience; the image is especially grievous because hoped-for benefits of spending turn to harm, like a ruined harvest.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:3:115-118/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:3:115-118/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:3:115-118/r3.claim: The example concerns lower-ranking Jews' spending on their scholars: it harms them as a freezing wind destroys the crop of people who wrong themselves through disbelief and sin.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:3:115-118/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:3:115-118/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:3:115-118/r4.claim: Their spending harms them, and God does not wrong them because everything he does with his creatures is just; they wrong themselves through disbelief and disobedience.

JISHUMI:v2p1282/r1.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v2p1282/r1.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v2p1282/r1.claim: Ghنى is the opposite of poverty: possessing what removes need; God cannot need because He is not a body and is powerful in Himself, with nothing able to disable Him.

JISHUMI:v2p1282/r10.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v2p1282/r10.speaker: أبو علي
JISHUMI:v2p1282/r10.claim: Another report says it concerns hypocritical spending by disbelievers alongside believers in war against the polytheists.

JISHUMI:v2p1282/r11.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v2p1282/r11.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v2p1282/r11.claim: A third reported occasion says Jewish commoners spent on their scholars.

JISHUMI:v2p1282/r12.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v2p1282/r12.speaker: مجاهد والأصم وأبو مسلم
JISHUMI:v2p1282/r12.claim: They say the verse concerns all disbelievers and all their worldly spending and charitable gifts.

JISHUMI:v2p1282/r2.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v2p1282/r2.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v2p1282/r2.claim: To relieve someone is to avert harm that otherwise would have reached them; one thing may also replace another in removing need.

JISHUMI:v2p1282/r4.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v2p1282/r4.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v2p1282/r4.claim: The word for Hellfire derives from light; it is a subtle body containing heat and light and having an upper dependence.

JISHUMI:v2p1282/r5.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v2p1282/r5.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v2p1282/r5.claim: Ṣirr is cold harmful to plants; ṣarṣar is a cold wind, with the root associated with sound, while others explain it as the sound of flame or a severe cold wind.

JISHUMI:v2p1282/r6.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v2p1282/r6.speaker: الزجاج
JISHUMI:v2p1282/r6.claim: Al-Zajjaj says ṣirr is the sound of a fire's blaze within that wind.

JISHUMI:v2p1282/r7.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v2p1282/r7.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v2p1282/r7.claim: A parable is a likeness that becomes proverbial through repeated use for similar cases.

JISHUMI:v2p1282/r8.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v2p1282/r8.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v2p1282/r8.claim: The comparison omits the word destruction: the sense is that destruction of their spending is like the destruction caused by a freezing wind.

JISHUMI:v2p1282/r9.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v2p1282/r9.speaker: اليماني
JISHUMI:v2p1282/r9.claim: One occasion report places the verse among the events of Abu Sufyan and his companions at Badr when they rallied against the Prophet.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v2p94#2/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v2p94#2/r3.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v2p94#2/r3.claim: The expenditure may mean Abu Sufyan's party spending at Badr and Uhud to oppose the Prophet, or, according to Muqatil, Jews' spending on their scholars.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v2p94#2/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v2p94#2/r4.speaker: مجاهد
BAGHAWI-FULL:v2p94#2/r4.claim: Mujahid says it means all the disbelievers' worldly expenditures and charitable gifts; another view means show-off giving that does not seek God's face.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v2p94#2/r5.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v2p94#2/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
BAGHAWI-FULL:v2p94#2/r5.claim: Ibn Abbas is reported to gloss ṣirr as a deadly hot wind; another view says it is a sound, while most exegetes say it is intense cold.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v2p94#2/r6.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v2p94#2/r6.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v2p94#2/r6.claim: The crop belongs to people who wronged themselves through disbelief, disobedience, and withholding God's due; ṣirr means a severe cold wind in the preferred majority explanation.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v2p94#2/r7.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v2p94#2/r7.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v2p94#2/r7.claim: Disbelievers' spending disappears when they need it, like a cold wind or fire destroying a crop before its owners benefit; God does not wrong them, they wrong themselves.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p432#2/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p432#2/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p432#2/r1.claim: Ṣirr is a cold wind, supported by poetry using ṣirr and ṣarṣar.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p432#2/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p432#2/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p432#2/r2.claim: The phrase may describe the wind as cold in an emphatic way, use ṣirr as a verbal noun for cold, or follow an idiom in which something is ‘in’ another, as in the cited line about God sustaining the weak.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p432#2/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p432#2/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p432#2/r3.claim: The spenders' wealth served status, public praise, and remembrance rather than God's approval, like a crop ruined by cold.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p432#2/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p432#2/r4.speaker: قيل
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p432#2/r4.claim: Another view says the comparison concerns what they spent to seek nearness to God despite their disbelief.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p432#2/r5.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p432#2/r5.speaker: قيل
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p432#2/r5.claim: Another view says their spending against the Prophet was wasted because it did not achieve their intended purpose.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p433/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p433/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p433/r1.claim: The crop owners' injustice makes its destruction a punishment, more severe than an ordinary loss because it comes from divine anger.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p433/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p433/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p433/r2.claim: The comparison is a compound simile, as in the parable of the fire-lighter; alternatively, it compares the destruction of spending to a wind's destruction or the spending to a destructive wind.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p433/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p433/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p433/r3.claim: A reading addresses the audience directly with تنفقون.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p433/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p433/r4.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p433/r4.claim: The pronoun in ‘God did not wrong them’ may refer to the spenders, who made their gifts undeserving of acceptance, or to crop owners who deserved punishment.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p433/r5.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p433/r5.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p433/r5.claim: The doubled reading ولكن means ‘rather, they wrong themselves’; omitting its object pronoun is allowed only in poetry.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p494#3/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p494#3/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p494#3/r1.claim: The simile pictures disbelievers' supposed devotional spending and its erasure at Judgment as a promising crop destroyed by a scorching wind.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p494#3/r10.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p494#3/r10.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p494#3/r10.claim: Ṣirr is the fire of Hell in its freezing region, which burns in a way resembling ordinary fire.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p494#3/r11.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p494#3/r11.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p494#3/r11.claim: Ḥarth includes crops and fruits, all produced through working the earth; a hadith groups zakatable property as money, produce, or livestock.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p494#3/r12.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p494#3/r12.speaker: جمهور المفسرين
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p494#3/r12.claim: They understand the crop owners' wronging themselves as sins against God, making the destruction a fitting and swift punishment.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p494#3/r13.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p494#3/r13.speaker: بعض أهل العلم
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p494#3/r13.claim: Some scholars hold that all worldly calamities result from human sins, so any crop destroyed by wind belongs to people who wronged themselves.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p494#3/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p494#3/r2.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p494#3/r2.claim: The comparison omits one member from each pair and then names the other, an especially eloquent compression; Qur'an 2:171 uses a similar construction.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p494#3/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p494#3/r3.speaker: عبد الرحمن بن هرمز الأعرج
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p494#3/r3.claim: Al-Aʿraj reads tunfiqūn in the second person, as an instruction to Muhammad to address them.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p494#3/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p494#3/r4.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p494#3/r4.claim: The majority understands spending as wealth spent in pious acts and in hostility to the Messenger, which the disbelievers regarded as devotion.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p494#3/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p494#3/r5.speaker: السدي
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p494#3/r5.claim: Al-Suddi says the spending refers to their outward statements that conceal the opposite.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p494#3/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p494#3/r6.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p494#3/r6.claim: This is weak because it makes the passage about hypocrites, whereas its context concerns disbelievers who openly match inward belief and outward conduct.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p494#3/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p494#3/r7.speaker: بعض المفسرين
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p494#3/r7.claim: Some interpreters take the spending as their deeds, such as disbelief, which nullify other good acts, though the metaphor of spending is strained.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p494#3/r8.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p494#3/r8.speaker: ابن عباس، جمهور المفسرين
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p494#3/r8.claim: They define ṣirr as severe, burning cold, also called al-ḍarīb by the Arabs.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p494#3/r9.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p494#3/r9.speaker: الزجاج
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p494#3/r9.claim: Al-Zajjaj derives ṣirr from making a sound and explains it as the sound of the fire within the wind.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p495/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p495/r1.speaker: المهدوي، بعض الناس
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p495/r1.claim: They take 'a people who wronged themselves' to mean farmers sowed outside the proper season.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p495/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p495/r2.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p495/r2.claim: On this reading, the farmers misplaced their agricultural work in timing or method, which makes the crop especially vulnerable to burning.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p495/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p495/r3.speaker: امرؤ القيس
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p495/r3.claim: His verse about a malicious person setting a green palm alight illustrates why destruction of a healthy crop is a fitting comparison.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p495/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p495/r4.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p495/r4.claim: The pronoun in 'wronged them' refers to the preceding disbelievers, not the crop owners, who were not introduced as people to be reproached; the final clause also points to present wrongdoing.

TABRISI:3:116-117/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:3:116-117/r4.speaker: مجاهد
TABRISI:3:116-117/r4.claim: The spending may refer generally to all the charity and expenditure of disbelievers in worldly life; other views specify support for fighting the Messenger, Abū Sufyān's spending at Badr and Uḥud, or Jewish commoners' support of scholars.

TABRISI:3:116-117/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:3:116-117/r5.speaker: author
TABRISI:3:116-117/r5.claim: The comparison omits the word for destruction: their spending is like the destruction of a crop by a severe cold wind, and the ellipsis is signaled by the verse's end.

TABRISI:3:116-117/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:3:116-117/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
TABRISI:3:116-117/r6.claim: Ṣirr is interpreted as severe cold by Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, Qatāda, and others; Ibn ʿAbbās also reports the alternative of a deadly hot simoom.

TABRISI:3:116-117/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:3:116-117/r7.speaker: الزجاج
TABRISI:3:116-117/r7.claim: Al-Zajjāj explains ṣirr as the sound of a flame carried by the wind, while another possibility is the crashing noise of the cold north wind.

TABRISI:3:116-117/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:3:116-117/r8.speaker: author
TABRISI:3:116-117/r8.claim: The crop owners are described as having wronged themselves through sins; another view says they planted in the wrong place or season, so the wind destroyed the crop as correction.

TABRISI:3:116-117/r9.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:3:116-117/r9.speaker: author
TABRISI:3:116-117/r9.claim: God did not wrong them by destroying the crop, or by killing and capturing them, because their wrongdoing and disbelief made them deserve it.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p444#2/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p444#2/r1.speaker: مجاهد
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p444#2/r1.claim: The verse describes the spending and charitable gifts of unbelievers.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p444#2/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p444#2/r2.speaker: مقاتل
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p444#2/r2.claim: The verse concerns lower-ranking Jews' spending on their scholars.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p444#2/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p444#2/r3.speaker: أبو الحسن الماوردي
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p444#2/r3.claim: Other views make it polytheists' spending at Badr or hypocrites' spending when accompanying Muslims to fight polytheists.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p444#2/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p444#2/r4.speaker: السدي
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p444#2/r4.claim: The spending is a parable for the unbelievers' deeds in their polytheism.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p444#2/r6.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p444#2/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p444#2/r6.claim: Another view takes sirr as fire; Ibn al-Anbari explains that fire is called sirr for its crackling when it blazes.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p444#2/r7.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p444#2/r7.speaker: ابن الأنباري
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p444#2/r7.claim: A third view takes sirr as the noise and movement of gravel and stones, as in the word for shoe-squeaking.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p444#2/r8.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p444#2/r8.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p444#2/r8.claim: Harth means cultivated land; “they wronged themselves” means sinning through disbelief, disobedience, and withholding God's due, or sowing out of season.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p445/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p445/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p445/r1.claim: God did not diminish their reward without cause; they brought loss on themselves by withholding God's due, and the image illustrates their works being nullified in the afterlife.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p445/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p445/r2.speaker: ثعلب
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p445/r2.claim: The verse starts with the wind while its meaning concerns the crop; Arabic can front one element while intending another, as in several Quranic examples and a poem.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p445/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p445/r3.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p445/r3.claim: The examples include spouses waiting after husbands die, an Arabic line about Ibn Abi Diyan, and faces blackened on Judgment Day: each begins with one phrase but means a later element.

RAZI-FULL:v8p169#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v8p169#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v8p169#2/r1.claim: The verse removes the suspicion that unbelievers benefit from spending on good works: their unbelief nullifies its reward, just as a cold wind destroys a crop.

RAZI-FULL:v8p169#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v8p169#2/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v8p169#2/r2.claim: The apparent mismatch between spending and a destructive wind disappears if the analogy compares only the central outcome, a compound comparison rather than matching every component.

RAZI-FULL:v8p169#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v8p169#2/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v8p169#2/r3.claim: If components must correspond, one may supply the sense: unbelief destroys their spending, or their spending is like a destructive wind, or the phrase refers to funds spent to harm the Prophet and erase earlier good works.

RAZI-FULL:v8p169#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v8p169#2/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v8p169#2/r4.claim: Al-Rāzī's own proposed reading takes the spending as funds used against the Prophet; that unbelieving expenditure cancels earlier good works just as destructive wind cancels a crop.

RAZI-FULL:v8p170#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v8p170#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v8p170#2/r1.claim: The analogy may also describe worldly failure: unbelievers spend heavily to assemble armies and endure hardship, then Islam prevails, leaving them frustrated and regretful.

RAZI-FULL:v8p170#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v8p170#2/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v8p170#2/r2.claim: If only some unbelievers are meant, proposed groups are hypocrites giving from fear or accommodation, Abū Sufyān's party at Badr, lower-ranking Jews funding rabbis' distortions, or people whose supposed worship is mistaken.

RAZI-FULL:v8p170#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v8p170#2/r3.speaker: ابن عباس وقتادة والسدي وابن زيد
RAZI-FULL:v8p170#2/r3.claim: Most exegetes and linguists, including Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatāda, al-Suddī, and Ibn Zayd, take ṣirr as severe cold.

RAZI-FULL:v8p170#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v8p170#2/r4.speaker: أبو بكر الأصم وأبو بكر ابن الأنباري
RAZI-FULL:v8p170#2/r4.claim: Abū Bakr al-Aṣamm and Ibn al-Anbārī interpret ṣirr as scorching heat or fire; Ibn al-Anbārī relates the sound of flames to the word, and both readings destroy crops.

RAZI-FULL:v8p170#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v8p170#2/r5.speaker: المعتزلة
RAZI-FULL:v8p170#2/r5.claim: The Muʿtazilites infer reward cancellation from the crop analogy; al-Rāzī's school answers that reward depends on God's promise conditioned on faith, which unbelief removes, and earlier arguments against cancellation were given in al-Baqara.

RAZI-FULL:v8p170/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v8p170/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v8p170/r1.claim: Spending may denote all deeds expected to benefit people in the afterlife, as other verses call deeds buying, selling, or spending; al-Rāzī prefers literal financial expenditure because the preceding verse mentions wealth and children.

RAZI-FULL:v8p170/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v8p170/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v8p170/r2.claim: The report most strongly covers all unbelievers: worldly-directed spending leaves no afterlife benefit, while afterlife-directed spending cannot benefit them because unbelief bars its reward.

RAZI-FULL:v8p170/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v8p170/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v8p170/r3.claim: Unbelievers may fund good works such as hospices, bridges, and aid for the vulnerable, yet find their charity erased by disbelief; this agrees with verses on deeds becoming dust, futile spending, mirage, and acceptance only from the God-fearing.

RAZI-FULL:v8p170/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v8p170/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v8p170/r4.claim: If their expenditure funds sins such as harming the Messenger, killing Muslims, and destroying their homes, its failure is even more evident.

RAZI-FULL:v8p171/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v8p171/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v8p171/r1.claim: ظلموا أنفسهم may mean they disobeyed and deserved their crop's destruction; unlike believers, whose sorrow can still increase their reward, unbelievers gain no worldly or afterlife benefit.

RAZI-FULL:v8p171/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v8p171/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v8p171/r2.claim: Alternatively, they planted in the wrong place or season, since injustice is putting things out of place; their misplaced spending plus the misfortune of unbelief makes it fruitless.

RAZI-FULL:v8p171/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v8p171/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v8p171/r3.claim: God did not wrong them by refusing their expenditure; they wronged themselves by attaching it to conditions that prevented divine acceptance.

RAZI-FULL:v8p171/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v8p171/r4.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
RAZI-FULL:v8p171/r4.claim: Al-Kashshāf notes a doubled-lām reading of لكن; it means they wrong themselves, while dropping an implied subject pronoun is not permitted outside poetry.

QURTUBI-FULL:3:117/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:3:117/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:3:117/r1.claim: The word mā can be a verbal noun or a relative pronoun with an omitted object pronoun; 'like a wind' means like a gust of wind.

QURTUBI-FULL:3:117/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:3:117/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:3:117/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas says ṣirr is severe cold; one etymology connects it to the sound of a harsh wind.

QURTUBI-FULL:3:117/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:3:117/r3.speaker: الزجاج
QURTUBI-FULL:3:117/r3.claim: Al-Zajjaj says ṣirr is the sound of flames in the wind.

QURTUBI-FULL:3:117/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:3:117/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:3:117/r4.claim: The verse compares disbelievers' spending, which is void and useless, to a crop destroyed by cold wind or fire after its owners expected a harvest; the meaning was also treated in al-Baqara.

QURTUBI-FULL:3:117/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:3:117/r5.speaker: رسول الله
QURTUBI-FULL:3:117/r5.claim: A Prophetic report says he forbade eating locusts killed by ṣirr; the commentary does not give a grading here.

QURTUBI-FULL:3:117/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:3:117/r6.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:3:117/r6.claim: God did not wrong the disbelievers; they wronged themselves through disbelief, disobedience, and withholding God's due. Another explanation says they sowed in the wrong season or place and were disciplined for misplacing things.

BAYDAWI-FULL:3:114-117/r6.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:3:114-117/r6.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:3:114-117/r6.claim: The spending compared here may be the disbelievers' religious or boastful giving, or the hypocrites' giving for show or from fear.

BAYDAWI-FULL:3:114-117/r7.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:3:114-117/r7.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:3:114-117/r7.claim: Sirr is intense cold, commonly used of a cold wind; the comparison is a composite image of a cold wind destroying a crop belonging to people who sinned.

BAYDAWI-FULL:3:114-117/r8.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:3:114-117/r8.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:3:114-117/r8.claim: God did not wrong either the donors by wasting their gifts or the crop's owners by destroying it; they wronged themselves by unbelief, sin, or spending without a valid aim.

BAYDAWI-FULL:3:114-117/r9.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:3:114-117/r9.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:3:114-117/r9.claim: One reading has lakin without a doubled nun; the impersonal pronoun cannot be omitted except in poetic necessity, as the cited line illustrates.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p174/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p174/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p174/r1.claim: The worldly spending may be for prestige, generosity, and good reputation, or an attempt to draw near to God while remaining unbelievers.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p174/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p174/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
NASAFI-FULL:v1p174/r2.claim: Ṣirr in the wind means severe cold.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p174/r3.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p174/r3.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p174/r3.claim: The wind-and-field image can mean a destructive wind consuming the crop, or the destruction of their spending as a wind destroys a crop; ṣirr is parsed as a genitive description of wind.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p174/r4.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p174/r4.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p174/r4.claim: The crop owners wronged themselves through disbelief, so its destruction is punishment; God did not wrong them.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p174/r5.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p174/r5.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p174/r5.claim: Alternatively, the pronouns refer to the spenders: God did not wrong them by rejecting their expenditure; they wrong themselves by failing to provide a basis for acceptance.

QASHANI:3:113-117/r5.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:3:113-117/r5.speaker: author
QASHANI:3:113-117/r5.claim: Worldly spending for desire, display, or human praise rather than God's face is like a freezing wind that destroys a field; wrongdoers' shirk and disbelief bring the loss, not injustice from God.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p306#2/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p306#2/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p306#2/r2.claim: Ṣirr can mean fiercely scorching cold or simply cold, with a poetic line using it for a north wind; Laylā al-Akhyaliyya also uses the compound ṣarṣar wind.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p306#2/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p306#2/r3.speaker: شاعر
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p306#2/r3.claim: An unattributed poem uses ṣirr for a biting north wind striking the dwellings, as lexical evidence for the cold-wind sense.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p306#2/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p306#2/r4.speaker: ليلى الأخيلية
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p306#2/r4.claim: Laylā al-Akhyaliyya’s verse uses ṣarṣar for the cold wind that fills the jars with fat, supporting the severe-cold interpretation.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p306#2/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p306#2/r5.speaker: ابن كيسان
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p306#2/r5.claim: Ibn Kaysān says ṣirr is the sound of a flame; al-Zajjāj chooses this sound-based derivation from ṣarīr and says it is the sound of fire in the wind.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p313/r10.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p313/r10.speaker: ثعلب
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p313/r10.claim: Thaʿlab says the comparison begins with wind although its meaning concerns the crop; al-Zamakhsharī chooses a compound comparison, while Ibn ʿAṭiyya sees two paired elements with the other pair members elided as a mark of eloquence.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p313/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p313/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p313/r3.claim: After saying believers will reap their good deeds in the next life, the text depicts unbelievers’ spending as fruitless and uncompensated.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p313/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p313/r4.speaker: مجاهد
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p313/r4.claim: Mujāhid says the verse concerns unbelievers’ spending and alms.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p313/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p313/r5.speaker: مقاتل
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p313/r5.claim: Muqātil says it concerns low-status Jews’ payments to their scholars.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p313/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p313/r6.speaker: قيل
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p313/r6.claim: Other reported applications are polytheists’ spending at Badr, hypocrites’ spending on a campaign with Muslims, offerings to God despite unbelief, or expenditure against the Messenger that failed its purpose.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p313/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p313/r7.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p313/r7.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī compares unbelievers’ spending for prestige, distinction, fame, and good repute, without seeking God’s face, to a crop ruined by frost.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p313/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p313/r8.speaker: ابن عطية
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p313/r8.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya describes their spending as a self-image of devotional charity that becomes scattered vanity, like a promising crop destroyed by a scorching wind.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p313/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p313/r9.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p313/r9.claim: The ma is apparently a relative pronoun with an omitted object; the comparison can be read as spending against wind or, in sense, against crop, with several rhetorical analyses.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p315/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p315/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p315/r1.claim: The apparent spending is money; al-Suddī’s reading as outward words hiding their opposite is weak because the verse concerns open disbelievers, not hypocrites.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p315/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p315/r2.speaker: قيل
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p315/r2.claim: Another view makes spending stand for all deeds, such as unbelief; Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls this sound despite the distant metaphor, and al-Rāghib says expenditure is singled out because it is what they most visibly displayed.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p315/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p315/r3.speaker: ابن هرمز
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p315/r3.claim: Ibn Hurmuz and al-Aʿraj read the verb in the second person, ‘you spend,’ as an instruction to address them.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p315/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p315/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p315/r4.claim: The singular rīḥ is used for punishment, while plural riyāḥ is associated with mercy; a report prays for beneficial winds rather than a destructive wind.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p315/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p315/r5.speaker: النبي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p315/r5.claim: A reported supplication asks God to make it beneficial winds and not a destructive wind.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p315/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p315/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p315/r6.claim: Ṣirr is the grammatical subject of the preceding preposition phrase; it may mean cold (Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, Qatāda, al-Suddī), a flame sound, or a fierce wind sound.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p315/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p315/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p315/r7.claim: If ṣirr describes the wind like ṣarṣar, the sense is intense cold, with an omitted noun or a figurative ظرف construction; Abū Ḥayyān regards the latter analysis as far-fetched.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p315/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p315/r8.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p315/r8.claim: The relative clause ‘struck the crop’ modifies the wind, and ‘who wronged themselves’ modifies the people; their sins make the destruction punitive and more severe.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p316/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p316/r1.speaker: جماعة من أهل العلم
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p316/r1.claim: A group of scholars holds that worldly calamities arise from a servant’s sins, supported by several Qurʾānic passages; on this inference, a wind-destroyed crop belongs to someone who wronged himself.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p316/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p316/r2.speaker: المهدوي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p316/r2.claim: Al-Mahdawī explains ‘they wronged themselves’ as planting out of season or using an improper method; the crop is specified because such damage is widespread and firmly established.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p316/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p316/r3.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p316/r3.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī and others say ‘God did not wrong them’ refers either to spenders whose gifts were not accepted or to crop owners whose fields were destroyed because of their sins.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p316/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p316/r4.speaker: ابن عطية
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p316/r4.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya prefers the pronoun to refer to the disbelievers already named as spenders, not the crop-owning people, since the latter were not previously mentioned and the next verb describes the current disbelievers.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p316/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p316/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p316/r5.claim: A noncanonical reading doubles the nūn in ‘but rather themselves wrong,’ making anfusuhum the subject and yazlimūn the predicate; dropping the pronoun is tolerated at the verse-end cadence, but a pronoun-of-affair analysis would require poetic deletion.

SAMIN-DURR:3:117#2/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:3:117#2/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:3:117#2/r1.claim: فيها صر may be a full subject-predicate clause, or فيها alone may modify ريح with صر as subject; the latter is preferred because simple adjectives are the norm.

SAMIN-DURR:3:117#2/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:3:117#2/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:3:117#2/r2.claim: صر may mean severe burning cold, as the cited line shows; it may also mean صرصر, a cold wind, as Laylā al-Akhyaliyya’s verse shows.

SAMIN-DURR:3:117#2/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:3:117#2/r3.speaker: ليلى الأخيلية
SAMIN-DURR:3:117#2/r3.claim: Laylā al-Akhyaliyya’s verse uses صرصر for a cold wind.

SAMIN-DURR:3:117#2/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:3:117#2/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:3:117#2/r4.claim: صر derives from tightening and knotting, as in صرة; أصر على means to persist.

SAMIN-DURR:3:117#2/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:3:117#2/r5.speaker: الزجاج
SAMIN-DURR:3:117#2/r5.claim: Some say صر is the sound of fire in the wind, from صر الشيء يصر صريرا; al-Zajjāj endorses this gloss.

SAMIN-DURR:3:117#2/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:3:117#2/r6.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:3:117#2/r6.claim: If صر means cold or sound, its location in the wind is straightforward; if it describes wind like صرصر, an omitted noun or figurative containment is needed, and the latter is remote.

SAMIN-DURR:3:117#2/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:3:117#2/r7.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:3:117#2/r7.claim: أصابت is an adjective of ريح, not صر, since ريح is feminine and صر masculine; the prepositional description comes first because it is nearer a simple adjective.

SAMIN-DURR:3:117#2/r8.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:3:117#2/r8.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:3:117#2/r8.claim: ظلموا modifies قوم; ظلمهم may refer to the crop owners, whose sins caused destruction, or to the spenders.

SAMIN-DURR:3:117#2/r9.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:3:117#2/r9.speaker: ابن عطية
SAMIN-DURR:3:117#2/r9.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya prefers the spenders as referent because the crop owners appear only in the comparison, not to explain or correct their wrongdoing.

SAMIN-DURR:3:117#3/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:3:117#3/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:3:117#3/r1.claim: The light لكن is adversative; fronted أنفسهم is an object for exclusivity, stressing that wrongdoing’s harm falls on the wrongdoers, and the order also suits rhyme.

SAMIN-DURR:3:117#3/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:3:117#3/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:3:117#3/r2.claim: Some read لكنّ with gemination, making أنفسهم its subject and يظلمون its predicate with omitted object يظلمونها to preserve the verse ending.

SAMIN-DURR:3:117#3/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:3:117#3/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:3:117#3/r3.claim: Another parse gives the particle an omitted pronoun of affair as its subject, with أنفسهم as the fronted object; grammarians disagree whether omission is limited to poetic necessity.

SAMIN-DURR:3:117#3/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:3:117#3/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:3:117#3/r4.claim: The cited line إن من يدخل الكنيسة يوما supports allowing an omitted particle-name beyond necessity, though some restrict the construction to poetry.

SAMIN-DURR:3:117#3/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:3:117#3/r5.speaker: السكائي
SAMIN-DURR:3:117#3/r5.claim: Al-Sukkāʾī is credited with parsing the hadith as إنّه من أشد الناس عذابا يوم القيامة.

SAMIN-DURR:3:117#3/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:3:117#3/r6.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:3:117#3/r6.claim: A competing analysis treats من as extra, yielding إن أشد الناس; Basrans generally reject extra من here except al-Akhfash.

SAMIN-DURR:3:117/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:3:117/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:3:117/r1.claim: ما may be a relative noun with object suffix omitted or a verbal noun; كمثل ريح is predicate, though comparing spending to wind seems odd because the intended image concerns the crop.

SAMIN-DURR:3:117/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:3:117/r2.speaker: الزمخشري
SAMIN-DURR:3:117/r2.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī resolves the mismatch as a compound comparison: the whole scene is compared with the whole scene, not individuals one by one.

SAMIN-DURR:3:117/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:3:117/r3.speaker: ابن عطية
SAMIN-DURR:3:117/r3.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya sees two paired comparisons with one member omitted from each pair because the parallel implies it; he calls this the height of eloquence and inimitability.

SAMIN-DURR:3:117/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:3:117/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:3:117/r4.claim: A third solution supplies a deleted مضاف; adding مهلك before ريح is clearer than before ما ينفقون because it avoids directly comparing the spent object to wind.

SAMIN-DURR:3:117/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:3:117/r5.speaker: الشيخ
SAMIN-DURR:3:117/r5.claim: Al-Shaykh’s estimate may also require a second omitted مضاف before ريح, yielding a comparison of two acts of destruction.

SAMIN-DURR:3:117/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:3:117/r6.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:3:117/r6.claim: If ما is a verbal noun, the verse compares spending that yields no benefit to such a wind, an abstract act compared with a perceptible thing.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p105#2/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p105#2/r2.speaker: مجاهد والحسن والسدي
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p105#2/r2.claim: Mujahid, al-Hasan, and al-Suddi identify the spending in this parable as the disbelievers’ spending in worldly life.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p105#2/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p105#2/r3.speaker: ابن عباس وعكرمة وسعيد بن جبير وقتادة والحسن والضحاك والربيع بن أنس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p105#2/r3.claim: Most cited authorities explain ṣirr as severe cold; Ata says cold and hail, while Ibn Abbas and Mujahid also report fire, which Ibn Kathir relates to cold’s burning effect.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p105#2/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p105#2/r4.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p105#2/r4.claim: The ruined harvest pictures God erasing the fruits of disbelievers’ deeds, built without a sound foundation, just as the wind destroys the crop.

BIQAI-FULL:v2p138#2/r10.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v2p138#2/r10.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v2p138#2/r10.claim: The comparison has two paired images: wind destroying the crop images spending's harm, while the ruined crop images wealth that yields no return beyond loss and effort.

BIQAI-FULL:v2p138#2/r11.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v2p138#2/r11.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v2p138#2/r11.claim: The analogy uses sensible wind damage to depict hidden, abstract wasted spending, and visible crop ruin to depict the intelligible loss of wealth after toil.

BIQAI-FULL:v2p138#2/r12.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v2p138#2/r12.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v2p138#2/r12.claim: The verse uses ellipsis by implication: the likeness of spending is omitted first because the wind supplies it, and the field is omitted second because spending supplies it.

BIQAI-FULL:v2p138#2/r13.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v2p138#2/r13.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v2p138#2/r13.claim: God does not wrong either group: disbelievers spent outside His prescribed way, while field owners failed to protect their crops through obedience; the verse suggests obedience can protect crops from calamity.

BIQAI-FULL:v2p138#2/r14.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v2p138#2/r14.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v2p138#2/r14.claim: The disbelievers' self-wrong remains their own even if their spending seems to spite believers: believers ultimately prevail, making that injury void and an added punishment for the spenders.

BIQAI-FULL:v2p138#2/r8.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v2p138#2/r8.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v2p138#2/r8.claim: Their spending, whether meant as worship or not, bears no fruit because they omitted sincerity, the condition by which it is accepted.

BIQAI-FULL:v2p138#2/r9.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v2p138#2/r9.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v2p138#2/r9.claim: The icy, destructive wind striking a field owned by people who wronged themselves through unbelief images their wasted spending and wealth, bringing toil and harm in both worlds.

DURR-FULL:v2p298/r10.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p298/r10.speaker: السدي
DURR-FULL:v2p298/r10.claim: The parable concerns polytheists' rejected spending: their associationism destroys it like a freezing wind destroys a crop planted by wrongdoers.

DURR-FULL:v2p298/r11.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p298/r11.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v2p298/r11.claim: Sirr in the wind means intense cold; Ibn al-Azraq asks whether Arabs use the word and Ibn Abbas says they do.

DURR-FULL:v2p298/r9.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p298/r9.speaker: مجاهد
DURR-FULL:v2p298/r9.claim: The spending described is the spending of a disbeliever in worldly life.

BURSEVI:v2p68/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v2p68/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v2p68/r3.claim: The verse answers the thought that unbelievers might benefit from charitable spending: they do not benefit even when they intend God's pleasure.

BURSEVI:v2p68/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v2p68/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v2p68/r4.claim: Unbelievers may spend for worldly benefit, afterlife reward, public praise, or hostility toward Muslims; Abū Sufyān and companions spent heavily at Badr and Uḥud.

BURSEVI:v2p68/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v2p68/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v2p68/r5.claim: Ṣirr is a devastating cold, originally a verbal noun but commonly used for a cold wind; it strikes the harvest of people who wronged themselves through unbelief and sin.

BURSEVI:v2p68/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v2p68/r6.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v2p68/r6.claim: The wind completely destroys the harvest, just as their spending vanishes without benefit; God does not wrong them, since they spent wrongly.

BURSEVI:v2p68/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v2p68/r7.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v2p68/r7.claim: Even if unbelievers built hostels and bridges or helped the weak, orphans, and widows hoping for reward, unbelief nullifies the good and leaves grief like a burned crop.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p36#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p36#2/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v4p36#2/r1.claim: The field’s owners wronged themselves by unbelief and disobedience, so God’s destruction was especially dreadful; alternatively, the phrase says only unbelievers lose both worldly and afterlife benefit, while others may be rewarded for patience.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p36#2/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p36#2/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v4p36#2/r2.claim: Another interpretation says they wronged themselves by planting in the wrong place or season; the crop was destroyed utterly, as punishment or correction for misplacing what belonged elsewhere.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p36#2/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p36#2/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v4p36#2/r3.claim: The comparison is composite, and its central point is waste and meager yield; a composite comparison need not place the thing named after the particle as the exact counterpart.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p36#2/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p36#2/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v4p36#2/r4.claim: Other parses compare the destruction of spending with wind destroying a field, or the spending itself with a destructive wind; a differentiated reading maps God’s destruction and the expenditure separately.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p36#2/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p36#2/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v4p36#2/r5.claim: The frozen wind makes the crop worthless, mirroring God’s rendering their deeds scattered; the focus is negligible yield and loss.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p36#2/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p36#2/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v4p36#2/r6.claim: The pronoun in ‘God did not wrong them’ may refer to the spenders, whose wasted expenditure was inappropriate, or to the field’s people, who deserved its destruction.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p36#2/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p36#2/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v4p36#2/r7.claim: A doubled-lām reading of lākin makes ‘themselves’ its subject and ‘they wrong’ its predicate with an omitted object; the light reading also omits the object, not fronting ‘themselves.’

ALUSI-FULL:v4p36#2/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p36#2/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v4p36#2/r8.claim: The shān pronoun would ordinarily not be omitted outside poetry; a poetic line about love is offered as evidence, though the author regards the analysis as difficult.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p36#2/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p36#2/r9.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v4p36#2/r9.claim: Fronting ‘themselves’ serves the verse ending, not exclusivity; the present tense indicates repeated, continuing self-wronging.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p36/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p36/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v4p36/r1.claim: The parable shows that wealth cannot help disbelievers; children need no separate explanation because unbelieving children share judgment, while believing children may oppose their parents and abandon them on Judgment Day.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p36/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p36/r2.speaker: مجاهد
ALUSI-FULL:v4p36/r2.claim: The relative mā represents all forms of disbelievers’ expenditure, whatever their kind; other views restrict it to anti-Prophetic spending generally, Quraysh at Badr and Uḥud, or subordinate Jews funding corrupt scholars.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p36/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p36/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v4p36/r3.claim: Rīḥ here is singular; ṣirr can mean severe cold according to Ibn ʿAbbās and others, while al-Zajjāj says a fiery blaze was present in the wind.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p36/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p36/r4.speaker: إبن عباس
ALUSI-FULL:v4p36/r4.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and others explain ṣirr as intense cold; a separate explanation makes it fire’s flare.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p36/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p36/r5.speaker: الزجاج
ALUSI-FULL:v4p36/r5.claim: Al-Zajjāj says ṣirr means a flame of fire that was contained in the wind.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p36/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p36/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v4p36/r6.claim: Treating ṣirr as a cold wind within a wind needs strained explanation; he favors its usual sense of cold, while recorded alternatives derive it from sound or a stormy cry but lack established usage.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p36/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p36/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v4p36/r7.claim: Some parse ṣirr as an adjective with an omitted noun, but deleting the noun is unfamiliar; another view takes the word as wind’s own sound, which is unattested.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p36/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p36/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v4p36/r8.claim: Rīḥ derives from a wāw-root and has plural forms arwāḥ and aryāḥ; the singular may also appear as rīḥa, like dār and dāra.

ALUSI-FULL:v4p36/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v4p36/r9.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v4p36/r9.claim: A tradition says one wind is associated with punishment and plural winds with mercy, prompting the prayer that it be winds rather than a single wind.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p61/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p61/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p61/r1.claim: The discussion of wind was given earlier at 2:164; here ṣirr is deadly severe cold that leaves plants looking burned, whereas ṣarṣar is a fierce wind that may be cold.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p61/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p61/r2.speaker: الكشاف
IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p61/r2.claim: Al-Kashshāf permits ṣirr to mean cold wind synonymously with ṣarṣar; Ibn ʿĀshūr rejects the usage because al-Asās and al-Rāghib do not attest it.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p61/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p61/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p61/r3.claim: Saying the wind contains ṣirr conveys exceptionally intense cold, as if it carried cold itself to the crop.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p61/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p61/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p61/r4.claim: Ḥarth is a verbal noun used for its object: cultivated land, meaning the crop or field that the wind struck; its meanings were discussed at 3:14.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p62/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p62/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p62/r1.claim: The phrase ظلموا أنفسهم is an inserted moral description that heightens condemnation, not part of the depicted wind-and-crop image; poets also add details that do not affect a comparison, as Kaʿb ibn Zuhayr does of water.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p62/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p62/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p62/r2.claim: Because listeners know the punishment of self-wrongdoers is severe, the phrase serves as admonition; the spending image explains why unbelievers' wealth and children cannot save them.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p62/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p62/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p62/r3.claim: God did not wrong the unbelievers by rejecting their spending: they caused this outcome by lacking faith, a condition for accepted deeds, after being informed and warned; this confirms God's promise not to wrong anyone.

TABATABAI:3:117-120/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:3:117-120/r1.speaker: بعض المفسرين
TABATABAI:3:117-120/r1.claim: Some exegetes assign this verse to polytheists and the previous one to Jews; the author calls that reconciliation mistaken.

TABATABAI:3:117-120/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:3:117-120/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:3:117-120/r2.claim: Ṣirr is severe cold; 'in this worldly life' shows these spenders are cut off from the afterlife, and their spending seeks only worldly affairs and corrupt aims.

TABATABAI:3:117-120/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:3:117-120/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:3:117-120/r3.claim: The crop is attributed to people who wronged themselves to connect with 'God did not wrong them': their corrupt spending brings misery and ruins what they mistake for happiness, like freezing wind destroying a crop.

ASAD-NOTES:3:117#n86/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:3:117#n86/r1.speaker: Zamakhshari
ASAD-NOTES:3:117#n86/r1.claim: Zamakhshari explains that deniers lose their entire worldly and otherworldly harvest, while believers retain hope of an afterlife reward for patience even when apparent gains are lost; the verse stresses the completeness of deniers' loss.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:3:117/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:3:117/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:3:117/r1.claim: The word sırr, rendered as scorching, can mean severe cold, poisonous heat, or blazing fire.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:3:117/r2.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:3:117/r2.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:3:117/r2.claim: The verse compares disbelievers' showy spending, pursuit of praise, or efforts to defeat Muslims to crops destroyed by a freezing wind.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:3:117/r3.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:3:117/r3.speaker: Şevkânî
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:3:117/r3.claim: One interpretation says disbelievers' showy spending is like crops reduced to dry stalks by a freezing storm: neither the crops nor the spending yields benefit.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:3:117/r4.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:3:117/r4.speaker: Şevkânî
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:3:117/r4.claim: Another interpretation says showy spending destroys the disbelievers' other good deeds and ruins their afterlife, like a freezing storm destroying young crops; it is compared to poison contaminating food.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:3:117/r5.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:3:117/r5.speaker: Mevdûdî
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:3:117/r5.claim: A third interpretation makes crops symbolize human life: deeds are harvested in the afterlife, charity can increase reward but disbelief can poison it, and misuse of God's wealth under His sovereignty can bring punishment.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:3:117/r6.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:3:117/r6.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:3:117/r6.claim: Spending to deny truth and stop others accepting it destroys good qualities and brings loss in this world and the next; Qur'an says disbelievers' deeds are lost in both.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:3:117/r7.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:3:117/r7.speaker: Râzî
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:3:117/r7.claim: Razi says interpreting the verse as worldly loss too is not far-fetched; spending one's valuable lifetime without attaining eternal happiness is itself a loss.

STUDYQURAN:3:117/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:3:117/r1.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:3:117/r1.claim: The wind image depicts disbelievers' actions in this life as unrooted and sterile.

STUDYQURAN:3:117/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:3:117/r2.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:3:117/r2.claim: The verse's cold wind contrasts with the burning wind in 2:266; 14:18 depicts disbelievers' deeds as ashes ready to blow away.

STUDYQURAN:3:117/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:3:117/r3.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:3:117/r3.claim: Elsewhere wind also has a nourishing dimension, as in 7:57, 25:48, 30:46, and 35:9.

STUDYQURAN:3:117/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:3:117/r4.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:3:117/r4.claim: The Quran repeatedly speaks of people wronging themselves.
